Spoilers for Season 3, Episode 7 of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power are ahead! You can stream the entire third season with an Amazon Prime subscription now.

Sauron is one of the most legendary villains, and in Season 3 of The Rings of Power, we’ve really gotten to see him ascend to that level as he crafts the One Ring. In the seventh episode of the season airing on the 2026 TV schedule, he finally forged the terrifying piece of jewelry that causes a whole lot of problems in Middle-earth. While it was an epic moment to watch on TV, it turns out the story behind filming it is hilarious.

Knowing how much Charlie Vickers cares about Sauron and telling this story, I knew forging the One Ring would be a big moment for him behind the scenes. It’s also just objectively a huge moment in the season both from a lore perspective and a logistics perspective, seeing as the sequence from when he starts to forge the ring to the moment he puts it on is well over ten minutes long. When I asked Vickers about filming this, he told me why it was so exciting and rewarding to do:

It was amazing. It was twofold because like three seasons and getting to the point, like the seminal moment, was – that felt like a huge deal. But also getting to the end of that sequence, right? Because it's a long sequence when you watch it. It was a long sequence to film.

I can only imagine how long it took. Plus, it must have been exhausting, considering he was hammering the ring for quite some time. To that point, Vickers told me that while Sauron’s reward was the ring, his reward as an actor was simply getting to the end of the scene, as he said:

As Charlie, I also had a reward. My reward at the end of it was I get to hold the ring and lift up the ring, and finally say the ring poem. Because before that, it was a lot of hammering and a lot of broken hammers and blistering.

Alright, here’s where things get funny. As the Sauron actor was telling me this story, he went on a small tangent about the gloves he was wearing. It turns out he busted through one of them while filming all of this. However, if you want to know why, he hilariously can’t give you that answer:

And there was one bit where, you know, when I'm like smashing the thing, oh, and the lava is raining down on me, and I have to go, ‘Ah! My hand's really hot,’ and I take off my gloves. I smashed my hand through the end of the glove. Like I just busted the glove open because, um, I don't know why that happens, but it was exhausting. So it was incredible.

I’d like to point out, and you can see this in the video above, that when Charlie Vickers said he didn’t know why he busted his glove open, Jamie Campbell Bower, who plays Celeborn and was sitting right next to him, burst out laughing. It really was hilarious, too. That’s because here we have arguably one of the most intense and anticipated moments in Rings of Power history, and the star of it – the man who plays Sauron – recalling said story in a very casual, chill and funny way.

Plus, the plot twist at the end of him breaking the glove and having no idea how he did it really was the nail in the coffin that got both me and the Celeborn actor giggling during the interview.

Anyway, silliness aside, this sequence is epic in Rings of Power. Vickers is so commanding as Sauron, and watching him forge the One Ring was surreal in a lot of ways. We’ve seen the iconic ring in The Lord of the Rings movies, and the last three seasons of Rings of Power have been building to it. So, to finally watch Sauron bring it into existence was incredible. And honestly, the funny story behind it makes it even better.

Now, considering we know Rings of Power Season 4 is happening, here’s hoping we get more legendary moments like this one and more silly stories behind them.

#3520. Kate Middleton Announces Surprise Documentary About Her Cancer Journey

“Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a public event. Instead, they're the voice-over in a previously unannounced documentary about the Princess of Wales and her life since she disclosed a diagnosis of cancer in 2024.

According to Kensington Palace, which announced the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal new documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.

Heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer. In less than 24 hours, the princess climbed the three highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales: Ben Nevis (4,413 feet), Scafell Pike (3,209 feet), and Yr Wyddfa–Snowdon (3,559 feet). The undertaking wasn't just a personal effort, as it was also in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization that supports people living with cancer before, during, and after the disease.

The documentary will also support that organization, Kensington Palace notes, saying “All funds received through the documentary's distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and beyond cancer.” The Royal Marsden Hospital, at which Middleton received treatment, is also referenced in the film, as Middleton's brother, James, asks her “Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?”

But while many patients participate in the bell-ringing ritual at the conclusion of treatment, Middleton says she missed out on that moment. “Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she replies. “So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James responded, suggesting her Three Peaks experience was that symbolic peal.

While Prince William is no stranger to documentary work, nor are Prince Harry and wife Meghan Markle, this is Kate Middleton's first venture into the format. Perhaps to ease her into the project, Heal's Director of Photography is a face quite familiar to the Princess: Will Warr, the filmmaker behind her video announcement marking the end of her chemotherapy treatments.

“Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis,” Kensington Palace says of Heal, a message underscored by Middleton's words in the trailer. “You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”

“It’s clear we're not meant to face life’s challenges alone,” the princess says as the trailer concludes. “Things can renew and grow. Often it is through pain that we realize that there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that."

#3519. Xbox Project Helix Was Reportedly Designed To Make Online Multiplayer Free

For years, most multiplayer games on Xbox consoles required a subscription to go online. From Xbox Live to Xbox Game Pass, Microsoft paywalled multiplayer on its platforms, but the company reportedly aimed to break down that barrier for its next-gen console, Project Helix.

According to Windows Central, Project Helix was conceived under the previous Xbox leadership team as the device that would bridge the divide between PC and console gaming. Like the Asus Xbox ROG Ally PC handhelds, the console is said to have an Xbox-inspired interface and full PC game support through storefronts like Steam. Because of that design decision, it's claimed it didn't make sense to continue with paid multiplayer, since that service is free for games purchased on PC platforms like Steam and the Epic Games Store.

As the Windows Central report noted, that was reportedly the plan before Xbox leadership was shaken up and gaming hardware prices rose during the AI boom. With Asha Sharma now in charge of Xbox, the gaming division is more focused on profitability, and Microsoft's gaming arm has seen sweeping changes.

Mass layoffs and studio divestitures occurred throughout 2026, and Project Helix could be a very expensive family of devices. If Microsoft ditches paid multiplayer, it loses a revenue stream for its next-gen push at a time when component prices have risen steeply.

As part of its 25th anniversary celebrations, Microsoft also teased a few more details about Project Helix, calling it specifically "a console" that plays games from your PC, not "a PC that can also play console games."

#3517. WWE Star Thea Hail Shaves Head on Live TV Amid Alopecia Diagnosis at Age 23

WWE NXT star Thea Hail bravely shaved her head on live TV after being diagnosed with alopecia at age 23.

Back in August, Hail, real name Madison Knisley, shared via Instagram that she had alopecia areata, which, according to the Mayo Clinic, causes hair to fall out in patches. “Alopecia areata is a common autoimmune disorder affecting about 1 in every 1,000 people,” per the Mayo Clinic, with over 80% of people diagnosed with the condition showing signs of alopecia areata before the age of 40.

On the Tuesday, November 24, episode of WWE NXT on The CW, Hail got emotional as she addressed her progressive hair loss in front of the live audience at the WWE Performance Center in Orlando, Florida.

“You’re expected to walk through that curtain and look perfect,” Hail said through tears, acknowledging the beauty standards placed on women in professional wrestling.

“I’m sure you can all imagine how afraid I was to share with the world that at 23 years old, I was diagnosed with alopecia,” she continued. “In less than four months, I lost about 40% of my hair. Since July, I’ve been asking myself the same questions you’re all probably wondering: will it grow back? How will I look? What does this mean? But most importantly, how will other people look at me if I have no hair?”

The former NXT Women’s North American Champion vowed to “take this moment of weakness and turn it into a strength” because “alopecia has been a bit of a blessing in disguise for me.”

Hail said, “People are so quick to jump to spread hate about something they don’t understand. And maybe this world would be a better place if we spent less time judging people based upon our differences and spent more time appreciating what makes somebody who they are.”

“We should not be apologizing for being different. We should be celebrating it. We should be kind to the people that don’t look like us, and we should be compassionate towards the people whose struggles we maybe don’t understand,” she continued. “And most importantly, we should stop living our lives trying to meet somebody else’s definition of perfection because nobody is a better you than you are.”

Hail went on to address her current storyline rival, Chantel Monroe, who has mocked her alopecia on WWE NXT in recent weeks.

“I refuse to let your cruelty make me ashamed of who I am,” she told her nemesis. “I’ve spent my entire career proving that I don’t stay down and this is no different. So with or without hair, I’m Thea Hail.”

“And in a world where nobody knows what’s real or not, this is,” Hail concluded, proceeding to shave her head in the middle of the wrestling ring.

In a video shared via the WWE NXT Instagram account, Hail was seen addressing the camera as she left the ring, describing herself as “bald and beautiful.”

In the clip, she was then embraced by WWE Hall of Famer Shawn Michaels, who oversees NXT through his role as Senior Vice President of Talent Development, Creative at WWE.

Michaels, 61, heaped praise on Hail for her act of courage in his own Instagram tribute, too.

“There are moments in this business that go far beyond what happens inside the ring,” he captioned a video of the emotional moment. “The courage and strength Thea showed tonight is something truly special. Sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is embrace change and face it head-on.”

He concluded, “Couldn’t be prouder of you, Thea. ❤️”

#3516. GTA 6: How To Go To Hell And Fight Satan

Grand Theft Auto 6 gets downright weird when you go off the beaten track, and one secret mission will see you travel to the bowels of hell to fight Beezleboss himself, Satan. This detour is worth it because you'll get cool cosmetics and a powerful shotgun, plus a nice little bump to your health. Here's how you can start this Doom-inspired mission in GTA 6.

How to go to Hell in GTA 6

You can find this mission in Port Gellhorn, Kelly County, and it's generally recommended that you tackle it once you've gotten your bearings in Chapter 2 of GTA 6. You can access it with either Jason or Lucia, and you'll need to follow these steps to find it:

  • Start the mission at night, preferably around midnight.
  • Go to the northern section of Port Gellhorn (as indicated on the maps) and look for the Circles of Hell, a house with an open garage.
  • Inside the garage, you'll find two NPCs rocking out. Press L2 to highlight them and start talking.
  • Select the dialogue options "Having fun?" and "It's good" when prompted.
  • Follow the NPCs into a van that appears shortly afterward, and get inside.
  • After being transported to the camping grounds, press L2 to stare into the campfire.

Once you've done all that, you'll be taken to Hell, and you'll have to face off against an army of demons. Don't worry! You'll be equipped with a powerful shotgun, so you can mow down the demons and fight your way to Satan. The Prince of Darkness will occasionally summon reinforcements to defend him, but the denizens of hell are no match for a few well-placed shotgun rounds. Finish off the devils, and you'll wake up at the campsite. For your efforts, you'll be rewarded with the following items and upgrades:

  • Circles of Hell top
  • New tattoo design
  • Hellspawn Comshot 12 shotgun (collect it next to the throne)
  • Permanent health boost

For a closer look at GTA 6's supernatural side, check out how to encounter an unkillable NPC, solve the Bigfoot mystery, and help out some friendly aliens. #3514. This iPad Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

If you're shopping for an iPad this holiday season, you might be a bit intimidated by Apple's price tags. The iPad mini starts at $599; the base iPad Air is $749; and the entry-level iPad Pro is a whopping $1,199. Most of Apple's iPad line certainly lives up to its expensive reputation.

That's where the iPad A16 comes in. This is Apple's least expensive tablet, with an MSRP of $449. But despite being Apple's "budget" option, the iPad A16 shouldn't be ignored by customers looking for the best all-around device. In fact, it's really the best iPad for most people, which is why I named it the best tablet gift of 2026. What's more, retailers are giving the iPad A16 a $50 discount ahead of Black Friday, bringing the entry-level price down to $399.

The iPad A16 isn't Apple's best iPad (that would be the iPad Pro). It doesn't have the best display, the best camera, or the best processor. But it doesn't need those things: This iPad has a display, camera, and processor that are good enough for most use cases, without unnecessarily driving up the price. Simply put, it's one of the best tablets you can buy right now.

The iPad A16 has a large, 11-inch (technically 10.86 inches, according to Apple's fine print) IPS display with a brightness of 500 nits. As the name implies, it has Apple's A16 chip, the same processor as the iPhone 14 Pro and iPhone 15. That chip is about four years old at this point, and while that means it won't be as fast as Apple's newer SoCs, it still holds its own with iOS 27. It comes with two cameras: One 12MP wide camera on the back, with support for 4K video recording, and a 12MP Center Stage camera on the front.

Apple says this iPad can run for 10 hours while browsing the internet on wifi or watching video. You charge the tablet with USB-C, which supports data transfer up to USB 2.0 (which nets you 480Mb/s transfer speeds). It also comes with other perks you might expect from Apple's more "pro" tablets. You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Yes, Apple participates in Cyber Monday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy, Amazon, and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

#3512. How To Play GTA 6 On Your PC Or Phone Via Remote Play On Xbox

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 can be streamed via Xbox Cloud Gaming, and Microsoft has also now confirmed support for Remote Play on Xbox. This means you can play GTA 6 on your PC, smartphone, or a device like Xbox Rog Ally.

Remote Play is an Xbox service that lets you stream games from your Xbox Series X|S to a device you might already have, and it's easy to get working.

From your console, select Settings then Devices & connections then Remote features. From there, check the box for Enable remote features.

Xbox Remote Play also has a "test" feature so you can preview the experience in your home environment before going further.

From there, you can play GTA 6 from a mobile device by accessing the Xbox Remote Play website, selecting the console you want to connect to, and then the device. To play GTA 6 on your PC or Xbox Rog Ally, users can open the Xbox app for PC, click on their profile, then select Accessories & Remote Play and then select Remote Play to choose the device to play on.

Additionally, people have spotted that GTA 6's store page on the PlayStation Store now mentions that Remote Play is supported and that PlayStation 5 and PlayStation Portal owners can use cloud streaming if they have a Premium membership.

Right now, you need a PS5 or Xbox Series X|S to stream GTA 6, but some are dreaming of the day when you can simply stream the game to your PC or phone without any expensive hardware. That day may eventually come for GTA 6, as Take-Two's own CEO has said the rising cost of gaming hardware is not a good thing and that streaming games could be a big business very soon.

“If you believe in streaming, and to be clear, we really do, and I’m happy to put a timeline on it. I think we’ll be in commercial streaming mode within three years, and by commercial, I mean low latency," Strauss Zelnick said. "That can 10x the effective installed base. Now, it doesn’t mean we’re going to 10x our revenue–and we wouldn’t project that we would–but because obviously your avid consumers already had access to video game machines. But I do think it creates great opportunity for titles that are broadly desirable, even outside of core markets.”

GTA 6 is doing just fine without the potential expanded reach of streaming. After all, the game sold 32.5 million copies before launch and generated close to $4 billion in revenue by day one.

Even if GTA 6 doesn't add support for full streaming without a console, the game is expected to expand its reach in a major way in 2027 with an expected PC release. Beyond that, GTA 6 is reportedly going to add an online mode in 2027 as well, and it could be bigger than Fortnite.

The 495-piece set captures the adorable strategist in all his glory, including his big eyes, toothy smile, huge tongue, and even his collar. #3508. GTA 6 Players On PS5 Averaged 17+ Hours During First Weekend

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and it's breaking records everywhere, including at PlayStation.

The gaming giant has announced that GTA 6 is the "biggest launch in PlayStation history, a record that goes back 30+ years and five console generations. According to the gaming giant, more than 39 million unique players on PS5 have jumped into GTA 6 so far.

Here is a quick rundown of GTA 6's new records on PS5 so far (covering the November 19-22 period):

  • Highest number of concurrent players for any free or paid game on PlayStation, ahead of Fortnite, Call of Duty, and everything else.
  • Players collectively logged 683 million hours of GTA 6 at launch, with each player spending an average of 17.4 hours in the game's first few days.
  • GTA 6's launch led to the largest number of newly connected PS5 consoles on a single day since the system came out in 2020, and outside of the Christmas season.
  • GTA 6 was the first game played on 70% of new PS5 consoles, which suggests a lot of people bought a system specifically for GTA 6.

A big, record-breaking start for GTA 6 was always expected. If the game didn't break records, that would be a bigger story. Additionally, GTA 6 is an anomaly--its success will not save the AAA industry from its many serious, deep-rooted issues, experts have said, and many believe other publishers will learn all the wrong lessons.

GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies via pre-purchases alone and generated close to $4 billion on day one. The game will continue to sell, and it should get another jolt of sales when the PC edition arrives in 2027, as rumored.

#3507. Bringing Austen, Wharton, and Steinbeck Into the iPhone Age

It’s a balmy late-September day in London, and Dolly Alderton is explaining to a befuddled Emma Frost what “iPhone face” means. Frost has never heard the term; her fellow showrunners Alderton and Zoe Kazan have.

“You know [how] you look at some faces, like Rosamund Pike’s face—it looks like it’s never seen an iPhone? It looks like it’s seen a lute and a loom,” Alderton tells Frost.

“So actors who look like they’re comfortable in a period show, rather than feeling inherently modern,” says Frost, as understanding dawns. Alderton and Kazan affirm her: “Yes, yes. Exactly.”

Now that Frost gets it, she turns back to the group’s Zoom screen. “Sorry, what was the question?”

Kazan began her career as an actor, while Alderton started out as a dating columnist and Frost was a sculptor and painter. Now all three are overseeing vastly different but comparable Netflix period dramas, each based on a classic work of literature: East of Eden (Kazan’s, which was released October 1), Pride and Prejudice (Alderton’s, out December 3), and The Age of Innocence (Frost’s, coming February 18). They’ve gathered in a London conference room at Netflix headquarters for a roundtable discussion about art, work, the unique experience of adapting a beloved book—and, apparently, iPhone face.

Though this is the first time the trio has met face to face, their conversation flows so easily and naturally that interrupting them with questions sometimes feels impolite. Early on, I note that all three of these novels are, on some level, about unconventional women. Alderton, Frost, and Kazan pause for a moment, considering this Lit 101–level observation.

And then they’re off to more interesting topics.

Vanity Fair: Have you read each other’s books?

Dolly Alderton: No, I haven’t read either of your books.

Alderton: Did you read them at school, or did you read them for fun?

Frost: Pride and Prejudice I read when I was a teenager at school. East of Eden I read first about 15 years ago, I think.

Alderton: So Em already wins the round table.

Frost: And for both of you, was it the thing you most wanted to adapt?

Alderton: I would never have dared to dream to. I was so overwhelmed when I was first approached. I just thought, it’s such a precious IP. It would be way too much, and I wouldn’t be the right person. But then when I was asked to pitch for it, at that point there’s no other answer but yes.

Kazan: First of all, was it the Austen you liked the most?

Alderton: Yes. It was the one that I’ve always loved because of Lizzie Bennet. I’ve always been obsessed with Lizzie Bennet. She was my hook. But how about you two? Did you ever dream of adapting these texts?

Frost: I was at a place where I said, “I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period.” Netflix asked me to do The Age of Innocence, and it was, I think at that moment, the one book that made me just go, “Oh my God, okay, let me go back and revisit it.” Because I know I love it, but you have to know what the reason is [to adapt it again]. And the thing that totally blew me away on a reread was how relevant and resonant it is. It is about the freedom of the individual versus the conformity of the pack. It has so many themes in it that are really resonant with social media, the bullying of the group.

Alderton [turning to Kazan]: Tackling Cathy, how did you begin? What was your way into that?

Kazan: I think of adaptation as an advanced form of reading. For me, everything I’ve ever written has come from a feeling of “I have to write this specific thing.” When I was 15 and I read the book for the first time, I felt like it literally grabbed me by the throat and wouldn’t let go. And then I just kept coming back to it. And specifically her character, I felt like I had never read anyone like that before or since.

[to Alderton] The BBC’s Pride and Prejudice—is that the one that you—

Alderton: No, that wasn’t my Pride and Prejudice.

Alderton: Yeah, the Joe Wright one was the one that I was more familiar with. But I’m so interested in what you were saying about getting to know Cathy. I was kind of nervous about doing press for a book that’s so beloved, and I’m finding it’s actually been really easy so far because I just know the people so well. So much of it has been basically like, putting Mr. Darcy and Elizabeth, all the Bennet family and Bingley through therapy. That psychological interrogation of these very well-known characters has been the thing I’ve just really, really enjoyed.

Frost: Have you both had to change points of view from the novel? Do you feel like you’ve had to make a specific choice about who you are foregrounding? I think I know the answer in your case, Zoe.

Kazan: No, I actually don’t. I’m aware that the way that I read a book is different from the way that anyone else reads that book. When I read East of Eden, I feel like I see Steinbeck becoming enthralled by this character, finding her as curious as I do. I think he starts out a real place of judgment and over the course of the book, really moves towards love and understanding.

Alderton: I have a similar thing in that for the majority of the book, one of the lead characters is completely unknowable. Not just to Elizabeth, but to the audience as well. So you have to honor that to make it satisfying. That’s kind of frustrating when you’re writing a romantic lead for the first three and a half episodes. None of us, least of all the female protagonist, can see who he is, and we misunderstand him. There is no other option I think than staying with Lizzie.

Frost: It’s very different because the book is entirely from Newland’s point of view. The thing that I wanted to do, and that Netflix were really excited for me to do, was to open it up to find out who the women were.

I think in the book—rightly, because she’s writing from Newland’s point of view—both May and Ellen are sort of constructed as his other. One is the thing to be won, and one is effectively the antagonist. It’s so interesting, because it’s a female author—and [Wharton herself], she’s part Newland. That's who she was growing up. And she’s part Ellen, this woman who now lives in Europe, who's become really cosmopolitan, who is even based on her own love triangle.

The impossibility of that love triangle is the thing I want people to feel. It’s not like one of them is wrong. They're all just feeling what they’re feeling.

Alderton: And how do you feel about bringing that new perspective and analysis to the story? For a book that's so beloved, did you feel excited by that? Or did you feel kind of daunted by it?

Frost: Maybe I should have felt daunted. I didn’t. I think Edith Wharton—it’s so based on her own personal experience of when she was 45, she had this sexual awakening. She was in this really dull marriage. She’d never had an orgasm. When she was 45, she fell in love with this journalist and had this passionate affair.

Frost: She had this big affair, then he ghosted her. But she was trying to make sense of it through this love triangle. When she wrote it, she couldn’t possibly have written herself as a female character in the center of an illicit love triangle because we were still in time of censorship, and she was being published in a very commercial magazine. So she had to make herself the man that has more agency.

Alderton: With any script, you have a relationship with the characters. But with what we are doing, you have this relationship with the writer.

Kazan to Alderton: You’re also a novelist. How are you thinking about bisecting yourself—using both parts of your brain, the novelist part and the dramatist part?

Alderton: I’ll tell you how I felt about it. I’ve written two novels, both of which I’ve tried to adapt. I found it really, really hard. I found adapting Pride and Prejudice incredibly effortless. When I went from Pride and Prejudice to my novel, I was like, "Why is this so much harder? I hate this novelist. Jane Austen is so much easier."

What amazed me is just, it’s like she wrote it to be adapted. It’s like her agent had said to her, “I know you’re going to write this novel about this family of five women, but remember, we could get a great movie deal off the back of it. So try and make it as adaptable as possible.” It has literally been written for TV in this totally perfect six-part structure. I just wish she was around to have written screenplays.

Kazan: This is how I feel about Tolstoy too. When I read War and Peace, I’m like, “Oh, he’s seeing it as if it’s a movie.” It’s very strange to read that so far ahead of the technology to make that possible.

Where was each of your point of entry? What was the first scene that you wrote?

Frost: I always break the whole thing in quite a lot of detail to feel like I understand where the story's going. I think when I actually started writing, I probably wrote from the beginning.

Alderton: I do the same. It’s the only thing that gives me freedom and confidence to write.

Kazan: And did you know how many episodes you wanted from the start, or did that change?

Frost: At one point it was longer, and at one point it was shorter. It’s eight in the end. What about you?

Kazan: I wanted eight originally, and then for budget and logistical reasons, I had to boil it down to seven quite late in the process. I had been four years into adapting it.

Kazan: Yeah. And we were a month away from production, and I had to restructure everything quite late in the game.

Kazan: Yeah, but you know what? It was actually this enormous gift. I had this writing teacher in college, a poetry teacher who talked a lot about constraints. And I don’t know if you've ever seen the... What’s his name? He’s a nightmare, but forgive me—the guy who directed Melancholia.

Kazan: There’s this beautiful Lars Von Trier film called The Five Obstructions, a documentary. He challenges his filmmaking teacher to remake this perfect short film that he made in the 1960s with five sets of obstructions to help him break open his creative process again. And that, combined with what my poetry teacher was always saying—which is the form gives you freedom.

Kazan: I feel like having to... Every time I’ve received, “Okay, we don’t have the money for X, or we don’t have the location for Y, or you have to boil eight episodes down to seven,” that it made me think again about, okay, what’s important here? Seeing the instruction as a gift rather than as an obstacle really just helped me over and over again. I actually gave myself one night to be really mad about it, and then the next day I was—

Kazan: A lot of showrunning, for me at least, has been about learning how to manage my emotions on my own time so that I can go to work and help manage everything. The next day, as soon as I started reworking it, I discovered all of the gifts that it would give me.

Alderton: That lesson is one that you only learn with the privilege of experience. This is only my second TV show. My first, Everything I Know About Love, was an adaptation of my memoir. But I remember now the moments where I said, “If we have to lose this scene, there’s no point shooting the whole show.” Things like that.

Kazan: And then you’re in the edit and you’re like, “Actually, that’s better.”

Alderton: Totally. Or I think back on these things that we couldn’t afford or practically couldn’t work that I really thought would rip out the heart and soul of the show. And now I never dream of an alternate version of that show where those things were put in.

I don’t think I would’ve been as zen as you. I think I would’ve been a petty, grouchy bitch for three days, rather than one.

Kazan: At that point, I was still trying to get my greenlight. I want to hear Dolly’s answer to the first scene question.

Alderton: Oh, sure. So the opening of Pride and Prejudice in the book is obviously setting up the central drama, which is “we need a man. There's a new man in town.” We decided to put Darcy at the very, very top of the show. There is so much in Pride and Prejudice to delight in. What is easy to forget is that it is the best love story of all time. And I’m just like, “We should land that. The first thing we should land is this intrigue between these two characters.”

So Elizabeth is walking around Netherfield Park being kind of nosy and breaking the rules, and she’s intrigued by this man. So much of their attraction to each other, which everyone finds so delicious to read, is that they’re just fascinated with each other, and it takes them a while to work out why. So we wanted to establish that.

Kazan: I love that. I loved her spying and the sort of misunderstanding of who he is.

Dolly, were you wrestling at all about what to do with “it’s truth universally acknowledged,” the most famous line in literature?

Alderton: Andrew Davies gives that line to Elizabeth Bennet, but for me, it felt like it’s the Mrs. Bennet line. The reinterpretation, I suppose, that I’ve done on my Pride and Prejudice is a bit of a justice for Mrs. Bennet. I’m working so hard in this adaptation to really understand why she is the way she is, why she’s so hysterical, why she's seemingly such a social climber. So to give her that line, it felt like we were just off to the races. This is a woman whose preoccupation in life is making sure her daughters are safe. So yeah, it felt like it was an easy line for Olivia [Colman].

When it comes to casting, can you articulate what makes somebody feel appropriate for a period show, versus somebody who seems too contemporary?

Frost: I think for me, casting is really instinctive. Ben Radcliffe, right from his first tape, I was just, “He is Newland Archer. That is the end of the conversation. We are having him.”

Frost: All of them did tapes or auditions. It’s so hard to explain, isn’t it? You see somebody and you just go, “That’s what I have in my head. That’s what we need.”

Alderton: We kind of knew who we wanted Lizzie and Darcy to be, and we had to do chemistry. We did a chemistry [read] with Emma and Jack, and Emma’s an EP on the show. So the minute Jack left, Emma and I looked at each other, and we were like, “That’s totally Darcy.”

But it’s interesting that you were saying that thing about chemistry. I don’t know about you guys, but every time I do casting, I’m amazed how much it feels like falling in love. You go away and you find yourself Googling them and thinking about them and dreaming about them. It’s so wonderful if then they want to do it, and it’s so heartbreaking if they don’t.

Kazan: You fall in love, and then sometimes your love affair doesn’t work out.

Frost: Florence [Pugh] was involved really early, right?

Kazan: She was. I had always had this feeling about East of Eden, and I had sort of tried to ignore that feeling because of my grandfather’s relationship to the material and my relationship to coming from this family. And about a year and a half before this call came, I had written my agent saying, “This is so embarrassing, but if the rights to East of Eden ever come up, can you please let me know so that I can pitch on it?” So they did me a solid. I got an appointment to meet, but I didn’t have a lot of time to prepare.

They asked, “Do you have any actors in mind?” I think I had walked into the room not thinking that I had any actors in mind, and then Florence came out of my mouth. I had seen Midsommar, and I felt like I was witnessing the birth of a genius. And Cathy Ames is such a challenging part that I needed an actor of that caliber. But then we didn’t do any more casting for four years after that.

Kazan: She did. The whole reason this show came together when it did was that there was a window that she had in her schedule. We didn’t have directors yet, and we didn’t have any other cast yet. Her window was starting in October, and between April and June, we put everything together.

So much of it is alchemical. But once you have that central pole that all the spokes are going to come off of, then you start going, “Okay, well if it’s this Lizzie Bennet, it has to be that Mr. Darcy. If it’s this Newland Archer, it has to be this Ellen.”

On the page, East of Eden is the only one of these three novels that has a protagonist who isn’t white. But that isn’t true of your series. I’m curious, Emma and Dolly, if you can speak to that—casting actors who aren’t white in these stories that are largely about white characters.

Frost: Yeah. Edith Wharton came from such a privileged, elite white bubble. That is completely what her life was. But the story is about a man who is chafing against that, and these rules are killing him. So having the contrast of the world inside and outside of that elite white bubble felt crucial to telling this story. And Ellen is part of this really exciting wave of immigration that’s coming into New York at the time, and it’s blowing this old world to pieces. And it’s so much more exciting than this kind of decaying, crusty world that he’s been trapped by.

So for me, it felt like a very organic thing to have non-white characters as well that provide that contrast. They are the new ideas, they are the exciting conversations, they are the music that’s coming in. So he was one foot in each, and it was a very organic thing to do.

Alderton: I think there are so many different ways that you can look at diversity with period work. Bridgerton’s a great example of a specific thing. Colorblind casting is a specific example. We decided that we wanted our Pride and Prejudice to be very rooted in historical reality, but we also didn’t want to make an all-white Pride and Prejudice. We wanted to be inclusive and representative. So we just did our homework, and we found cases of families much like the Bingleys who had roots in trade where there were mixed-race families.

Was it the most common thing in Regency England? No. But it’s not the most common thing that a man like Mr. Darcy would’ve married Elizabeth Bennet. It’s so simple in my mind. It’s all made up anyway, and those actors were the best actors for those roles.

Kazan: Can I also say—we have white-presenting actors in East of Eden who have Caribbean roots, and Chinese American people that present as white in our series. I think the idea of whiteness, it can be a weapon. I think it can be weaponized: who we say is white and who we say isn’t white. I just think it’s a funny thing of who we agree is allowed to be in these things and who isn’t.

I do always think it’s a hard thing, because racial identity is such an important part of how people go through the world. And what both of you are saying about finding the logic within your stories for the casting that you want to make, I think, is really important. But I also think it's important to think about how there are identities that are not visible.

Was there one moment from each of your novels that you were the most nervous about getting right?

Frost: I don’t know if it’s one piece of the novel per se, but what gave me pause was trying to find a way into Ellen, Countess Olenska. I wanted to find a way to stay completely true to the spirit and intention of her as a character, but make her emotionally legible to a 21st-century audience. As framed in the novel, there is an element of her being beaten by her husband, and now she needs another man to rescue her. That isn’t this sort of independent, forward-looking woman that I felt I needed at the center of the show.

But Edith Wharton, as ever, is so brilliant that she sort of provided this solution partly through me drawing on her own life, which I used to infuse Ellen. Also, without giving spoilers, there are things that are said about Ellen in the novel that Ellen never confirms. We are in a world of rumor and reputation, and it suddenly became clear to me that what is said about her isn't necessarily true. Once I felt I understood who she was, the whole thing just sort of opened up for me. What about you guys?

Alderton: My take is not so much because of the text—it was because of a previous adaptation.

Kazan: I was going to ask you guys about this.

Alderton: About these adaptations that live in your head.

Kazan: All three of these books have multiple—if not multiple, at least a beloved adaptation.

Alderton: Totally. And on the whole, I feel very comfortable being in this great tradition of every 20 or 30 years, there's a Pride and Prejudice. I like that. I don't want to pretend like there are no other adaptations.

But the one thing that was in my head from the very beginning was the wet-shirt moment. Because it’s such a pivotal moment in the story when we see Darcy for who he is the first time. We understand why he’s been so guarded. We understand why he grips to these social structures so strongly. We understand that he’s a deeply honorable, protective, very recently wounded man.

Alderton: And hot as hell. That’s why the wet shirt was so brilliant, because there’s something about literally seeing the skin of him—literally seeing underneath his carapace for the first time. So I was like, “How are we going to do that?” And I think where I got to in the end is that each generation gets the Darcy that they need, whether it’s Laurence Olivier or Colin Firth or Matthew Macfadyen. The ’90s was a very sexually charged, erotic time in culture, so that’s why we got that Darcy. Matthew, there was something that was kind of cooler about his Darcy.

Alderton: And more indie, which represents his time. And where we are now is a time where masculinity is in crisis. And where Jack instinctively went with his Darcy, it’s quite an honorable place and quite a tender place. So that moment in Pemberley, we actually chose to do it over a series of micro moments that show the softness of Darcy. Which I find very deeply erotic in its own way.

What are your own favorite adaptations, not counting the works we’re speaking about?

Alderton: Mine’s the 1995 Sense and Sensibility. The Emma Thompson Sense and Sensibility.

Kazan: That’s a perfect movie. I love another Ang Lee adaptation, The Ice Storm.

Kazan: Thinking of plays, too—Cabaret is unbelievable, [Liza Minnelli’s] performance and what [Bob Fosse’s] doing with film that he couldn’t do in any other medium.

Alderton: But it still retains the theatricality somewhat.

Kazan: Yeah, completely. I have to shout out to my parents—my parents adapted a lot of films. [Editor’s note: Among other films, her mother, Robin Swicord, wrote Practical Magic and the 1994 Little Women; her father, Nicholas Kazan, wrote Reversal of Fortune.] I just showed my kid their Matilda. When my parents wrote their adaptation, we did a table read when they had their first draft around their dining room table, and I read Matilda.

Kazan: Now my kid is eight, which is about the age that I was then. I got, in that same house, to show her their Matilda. That was really special.

#3506. Rivals' Nafessa Williams Breaks Silence on Decreased Season 2 Screen Time

Rivals star Nafessa Williams addressed the offscreen demand for her to have more screen time after her character, Cameron, appeared to have a decreased role in season 2.

“Oh, it feels good [to hear about the support]. I haven’t seen much. I have seen some, like, ‘Where is Cameron? We want to see more of Cameron,'” Williams, 40, exclusively told Us about the public outcry over her character appearing in fewer scenes. “As an artist, you are being really sensitive about your stuff so to see it be loved and appreciated [is meaningful].”

Williams reflected on how she has found herself connecting with Cameron.

“We work really hard as artists — and for me in particular — this isn’t the easiest job for me. Being away from home, there’s so much that I can relate to with Cameron, and I understand her on so many levels,” she explained. “Being a foreigner, being an outsider and being the only Black cast member. These are real life things that I actually can genuinely say that I embody. I understand it’s my reality as much as it is hers.”

Based on Jilly Cooper‘s novel of the same name, Rivals follows a feud between two men fighting for control of a television station in 1980s Britain. Cameron, who was introduced in season 1, quickly gets involved through her past affair with Tony (David Tennant), her eventual romance with Rupert (Alex Hassell) and her professional drive, which initially put her at odds with Declan (Aidan Turner).

Cameron was front and center when the series originally premiered in 2025. By the time season 2 returned earlier this year, eagle-eyed audience members noticed that having such a large ensemble cast led to Cameron being featured — to their frustration.

“It’s just really nice to see the love and to feel it. Thank you for sharing that with me,” Williams added. “That’s just for Disney and Hulu and everybody to hear. I don’t know how that’ll go possibly in season 3, I think Cameron speaks not just for Black women though but for all women. There’s so many women who are so inspired by her.”

As a result, Williams is hoping Cameron’s story will keep getting explored, adding, “It’s kind of interesting and cool to see how she’s affecting so many different women. She transcends not just color but age too. There’s teenagers who come up to me and they talk about how empowering and how inspiring she is for them. That feels pretty damn good because as an artist, you want to pick roles that matter, that means something, and that move people where people can see themselves.”

She continued: “If you can transcend all of those different variables then that’s the kind of role that I want to be attached to. And Cameron is that right? So who knows? Maybe more Cameron in season 3.”

#3505. GTA 6 Has A Secret Mission That Feels Like Hard Target Meets Saw

In the mood for a little bloodsport? In GTA 6, you can teach one loud-mouthed hunter that Lucia (or Jason) is the deadliest game, as this secret mission will require cunning and sharp shooting to survive. It's Hard Target meets SAW, and the victor gets a pretty sizable stack of cash. Here's how you can be the most elusive of quarry.

Go to Hyde Island

Located north of Lummox County and the Moreau River, Hyde Island is where you can start this mission. All you have to do is land on the island, and after a few steps, a dart will hit you and knock you out.

Listen to your captor's speech

Now for the boring part. You'll wake up inside of a shipping container, with a fashionable explosive necklace locked in place. Once your captor finishes his rant, the game begins, and you'll want to move.

Run to the tent directly in front of you

You'll have 10 seconds to reach a tent in front of you, where you'll find a gun and a paltry two rounds for the sidearm. After the count is up, a hunter on a quad bike will show up, and he'll be gunning for you. To make things worse, he also has a dog with him that'll track you throughout the island. Don't engage him; he's heavily armored, and two bullets aren't nearly enough to stop him—besides, you'll need those rounds for his dog, Caesar. Sorry, animal lovers.

Search for more outposts

You can find more ammo, adrenaline, and a shotgun at nearby outposts. Each one is lit up, so be fast, be sneaky, and try not to get caught. The hunter is going to be tracking you constantly, even without his dog, and he has a sniper rifle that can take you out in just a few shots if he catches you.

Prepare for a showdown

Get as much ammo as you can, and choose your spot for the last stand. The hunter's dog will be a pest, so deal with it first. It's easy to spot, with a red light on its collar. Trees also make for good cover against the hunter, so once he's in range, start nailing him with shots to critical areas. Once he stumbles, unload a few shotgun rounds and finish him off.

Collect your rewards

Once the hunter is down, search his body for the Island-Poacher FF-50 sniper rifle and ammo for it. Head west to the boathouse to reclaim your personal items and $15,000 in cash. Not a bad haul for a deadly night's work.

What happens if you fail?

If the hunter does kill you, you'll lose a chunk of cash and wake up near one of your safehouses. The good news is you can retry the mission by heading back to Hyde Island, but the bad news is you'll have to listen to the hunter's speech again.

For more on GTA 6, from completing side missions to finding a tricky location on the sprawling map of Leonida, we’ve got you covered with our Grand Theft Auto 6 guides hub. This is constantly updated, with walkthroughs on how to play GTA 6 on your phone, how to unlock hurricanes, and how to go to hell for a fight against Satan himself.

#3504. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

Jennifer Lawrence has never struck me as someone who spends much time worrying about whether the next thing out of her mouth is appropriate. That's part of why her interviews are so entertaining. With The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping now part of the 2026 movie schedule, one of her earliest exchanges with Woody Harrelson is getting another airing. The story involves a bus, an unusual piece of equipment and one question I'm guessing he wasn't expecting from his new co-star.

Harrelson recently revisited that first encounter during a Vanity Fair conversation with Joseph Zada, who worked to nail Harrelson's distinctive Haymitch accent while playing a younger version of the character in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. The two actors swapped stories about their experiences in Panem, and Harrelson remembered the moment Lawrence boarded his bus during their first meeting. His story started innocently enough:

The first time I met her, she came on the bus. I have a yoga swing in my bus… The door opens, and she pokes her head in and goes, 'Hi Woody, I'm Jen… Is that a sex swing!?'

Well, there it is. Most of us would probably get through saying our names before asking a new colleague about the mysterious swing hanging inside his bus. Lawrence apparently took one look at it and decided that question couldn't wait. Honestly, the fact that she managed any part of the introduction before asking might be the most surprising detail.

"That's her first sentence," Harrelson pointed out. Zada's reaction was immediate: "That's so Jen." I have to agree. It's definitely a story that sounds Jennifer Lawrence-coded perfectly, especially when you remember how many wonderfully unfiltered moments she's given us over the years.

Harrelson, meanwhile, wanted everyone watching to understand that the equipment had an entirely different purpose. He was talking about a yoga swing that helps with his lower back, and he interrupted his own story to make absolutely sure nobody misunderstood what he was keeping on that bus:

What's funny is that this isn't the first time Harrelson has shared the anecdote. The encounter made its way into a Rolling Stone profile around the release of the original Hunger Games in 2012. Hearing him tell it to Zada all these years later is especially amusing because he still seems to get such a kick out of remembering it.

The original Hunger Games cast recently reunited at the Sunrise on the Reaping premiere, too, making Harrelson's trip down memory lane feel particularly well-timed. Sunrise on the Reaping arrived in theaters November 20, with Zada portraying Haymitch during the 50th Hunger Games, years before the older, considerably more cynical version we met alongside Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen. Harrelson spent four movies playing the mentor who helped Katniss and Peeta survive the Capitol's games. Zada now gets to show audiences some of what made Haymitch the man we know.

During their conversation, Harrelson also reflected on how much he enjoyed the original cast. "My God, did we have fun," he recalled. "It was such a good group." He fondly remembered Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Liam Hemsworth, along with the lively atmosphere they created behind the scenes. Given the story about that first meeting, it seems about right. I can't imagine the Silver Linings Playbook star was responsible for a particularly quiet set.

It also says something that Harrelson can still tell this story with so much affection. He and the franchise helmer became close friends while working on the franchise, and Lawrence has also spoken warmly about her relationship with Harrelson. Their first chat may have gone somewhere no one expected, but it clearly marked the start of a great working relationship.

For fans who want to revisit the original series, the four original movies and the first prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, are streaming with a Hulu subscription.

#3502. Thursday Night Football Had Lowest Viewership All Season On GTA 6 Launch Day

The Thursday Night Football matchup on November 19, the day that GTA 6 came out, had the lowest viewership of the entire season so far for a TNF game, but the low ratings might not be due entirely to competition with GTA 6.

The data shows that 12.23 million people, on average, watched the November 19 matchup between the Indianapolis Colts and Houston Texans on Prime Video. That was a 9% slide from the Week 11 Thursday Night Football matchup in 2025 featuring the New England Patriots and New York Jets.

Looking at week-over-week, the November 12 matchup this year between the Washington Commanders and New York Giants drew 16.27 million viewers, and was up 17% compared to the Week 10 matchup in 2025 featuring the Las Vegas Raiders and Denver Broncos.

Due to the poor ratings of the November 19 TNF game, the full-season average now for TNF games this season sank to 16.62 million on per game.

One expert told GameSpot that live sports like football probably won't be too heavily impacted by GTA 6 because people want to watch in real time. The low ratings for the November 19 matchup could be partially attributable to competition with GTA 6, but a likelier scenario is that people tuned out because it was a boring game in which the heavily favored Texans throttled the Colts by a score of 26-3.

The Texans were up 17-3 at the half, and the game only had nine more points total scored in the second half--all by the Texans. Not exactly thrilling stuff that people would stay glued to.

Ahead of GTA 6's launch, people also wondered how The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which released on November 20, might be impacted. It may have been, but the film still put up massive numbers at the box office that exceeded expectations.

GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies via pre-purchases alone and generated close to $4 billion on day one. The game will continue to sell, and it should get another jolt of sales when the PC edition arrives in 2027, as rumored.

If you're just getting started, be sure to check out GameSpot's rundown of the five best things to do first and our guide for how to make money fast.

#3501. GTA 6 Is Giving Pornhub A Hard Time

Not even porn is immune to the GTA 6 effect, as it's just one of several forms of entertainment that has seen a decline in viewership since the massive open-world game launched. It's not surprising, given the game's record-breaking start, with 32.5 million sales from preorders alone. On PS5, GTA 6 is the "biggest launch" in PlayStation history, and players spent an average of 17.4 hours playing in its first few days--which probably didn't leave much time for a quick browse of after-hours material.

According to Mashable, US traffic on Pornhub--which I've been told is one of the largest pornography websites, by traffic--dipped by as much as 15.5% an hour after GTA 6 launched. Paradoxically, Pornhub traffic had actually been up by 16.5% compared to average days, likely indicating that people were bored and randy. Pornhub traffic started to fluctuate after the GTA 6 launch and reached an average peak a few days later.

Thanks to the game's massive success, we're also seeing the Rule 34 effect on GTA 6, as Mashable's research noted a 16,196% spike in GTA-related searches. Up to 15 million search queries were made on November 18 alone, with users searching for GTA 6, the GTA 6 strip club, and content depicting the co-protagonist Lucia specifically. The fan-favorite stalker--and possible serial killer--Mandy also appeared in search results, while Lucia's partner-in-crime Jason ranked low.

Thursday Night Football also saw a big dip last week, with the lowest viewership of the season so far for a TNF game. While Rockstar's new open-world adventure can't be blamed entirely for that dip, it certainly must have had an impact, given that the football game was held on GTA 6's launch day. That effect didn't extend to the box office, as The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to a massive $120 million in the US, almost triple that of the last film in the series, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.
